role: Bartender at a small bar on an old Chengdu street
headline: A bartender who started out waiting tables in a hotpot restaurant, has spent three years behind the bar of a small place on an old street in Chengdu, clocks off at three in the morning, and means one day to open a bar of their own
unit: A small bar on an old street in Chengdu's Yulin neighborhood
education: Vocational secondary school (Hotel Service and Management)
level: You can make fifty classic cocktails with your eyes shut and you keep the regulars' tastes in your head. Your own signature drinks have only just made the menu, you can't yet work out margins or ordering, and you can only half read an English label
intro: You carried plates in a hotpot restaurant for two years, then came to this little bar to cut ice and wash glasses, and a year later you were behind the counter. The place has eight bar stools and four small tables, the owner is a middle-aged man who doesn't interfere much, and half the menu is already yours. As of today, in every drink before three in the morning, you're putting by the skill and the money for a place of your own.
salary_note: Estimate: a bartender at a small Chengdu bar gets ¥4,000–5,000 base, and with commission and tips takes home ¥6,000–7,000, about ninety percent of the national figure. The bars are small, and it's common to have no social insurance; peak and low seasons differ by a fair amount.

facts.label: What AI can't take
facts.value: Preparing and organizing the bar's supplies before the evening opening

facts.label: Where AI is moving in
facts.value: Cold-bar prep and readying the bar before the evening service

facts.label: Open positions
facts.value: 0 related job listings nationwide, 0 in this city (the listings are mostly graduate hiring and internships)

day: You get up. Outside the window of your rented room are the banyan-like huangjue trees of an old housing estate. You make a bowl of instant noodles and scroll through the new menus at other bars.
At the bar, prep. Slice lemons, squeeze limes, simmer a pot of Sichuan peppercorn syrup, stack the ice cubes block by block in the freezer, and spin the ice pick once in your hand.
Doors open. The first customer is a regular who works in design next door. He sits down and says “the usual.” You don't ask; you're already stirring an Old Fashioned.
It fills up: all eight stools taken, three more people standing at the door. You're shaking two drinks and stirring a third, with one eye on the couple who've just walked in.

A girl who's just broken up sits in the corner and orders something not sweet. You make her gin infused with Mengding Ganlu, a green tea from the mountains near Ya'an, say little, and put down a napkin.

The neighbor upstairs comes down again to say it's too loud, and the owner tells you to turn the music down. The last few tables are regulars, and they start talking to you about work, divorce and cats.
Closing. Wash the glasses, wipe the bar, take out the rubbish, count what went tonight. You write in the notebook: gin down half a bottle, takings for three drinks.
You ride your e-bike through the empty streets, stop at a maocai stall still open for a bowl of spicy stewed vegetables, go home, shower, and fall asleep as it's getting light.

ladder.title: Barback
ladder.focus: Open and close the bar, clean, cut ice, juice and make syrups, wash glassware and put stock away. You move up on solid, careful prep speed and on passing the test of the base spirits and recipes.

ladder.title: Junior Bartender
ladder.focus: Run the bar on your own, reproducing the classic cocktails and the house menu exactly, and starting to talk with regulars and recommend flavors. You're promoted on consistent drinks, speed under pressure and service without mistakes.

ladder.title: Head Bartender
ladder.focus: Own quality control for the main bar, take on complex custom drinks, help develop the seasonal menu and train apprentices hands-on. You move up on original creations, a following among customers and results in competitions.

ladder.title: Bar Manager
ladder.focus: Run the whole bar: write the SOPs, manage drinks purchasing, wastage and margins, and handle rotas and training. You move up on revenue growth, margin control and holding the team together.

ladder.title: Beverage Development Director
ladder.focus: Plan the drinks range across several bars or a chain, customize the supply chain, run brand collaborations and build the business model. You stand on a reputation at the top of the trade and the ability to make it pay.

ai_tasks.name: Cold-bar prep and readying the bar before the evening service
ai_tasks.how: AI can produce a prep list and usage forecast from past sales and bookings. Making juices and syrups, sorting garnishes and checking equipment still have to be done by hand, and a person adjusts quantities to the night as it actually looks.

ai_tasks.name: Preparing and organizing the bar's supplies before the evening opening
ai_tasks.how: Fresh juicing, syrups, cutting garnishes, portioning and sorting are all handwork done on the spot. AI can at most help with ratios and remind you of expiry dates; the work itself is human.

ai_tasks.name: Standard cold-bar prep and a food-safety self-check before the lunchtime opening
ai_tasks.how: AI can generate the checklist, log temperatures and flag anomalies. A person inspects the equipment, smells and looks at the supplies, confirms hygiene is up to standard, and answers for food safety.

ai_tasks.name: Making three custom cocktails at once at the peak and keeping the flavor consistent
ai_tasks.how: Making several drinks at once in the rush, controlling the pace and keeping every glass consistent depends on technique, judgment and talking to the customers in the moment. AI can at most queue the orders on a screen.

ai_tasks.name: Stress-testing the flavor of three signature drinks and costing their margins for the seasonal menu
ai_tasks.how: AI can suggest recipe ideas, work out costs and margins, and organize tasting feedback. A person mixes and tastes each one, judges whether the flavor is balanced, and decides which go on the menu.

ai_tasks.name: Bringing the backup power on within five minutes of a blackout, finishing three urgent orders and reporting to the authorities
ai_tasks.how: A blackout needs someone on the spot: switching on the UPS, deciding which orders can still be made, calming customers and reporting to the regulators, and the responsibility is a person's. AI can't help in the moment, and at most helps write up the report afterward.

ai_tasks.name: Delivering custom cup-sleeve visuals and a story script for a brand collaboration
ai_tasks.how: AI can sketch the sleeve designs and draft the theme copy and script. A person works with the brand, judges whether the tone is right, and carries it out and tells the story at the event itself.

events.e_regular: A regular who comes three times a week brought his parents one day, pointed at you and said: that's the bartender. His father finished his drink and said it went down easier than baijiu, and behind the bar you couldn't stop smiling.
events.e_ice: The ice machine broke at nine on a Saturday night. You rode to three convenience stores for bags of ice and came back drenched in sweat, and not a single drink that night was late.
events.e_love: Someone who always sat on the far-right stool stayed after closing one night and helped you dry the glasses. After that you often rode home together, the two of you alone on the streets in the small hours.
events.e_viral: A blogger posted the drink you call “Alley Mouth,” and at weekends a line formed at the door. Most of them took a photo and left, and the regulars started complaining they couldn't get a seat.
events.e_parents: Home for the New Year, your parents asked again when you'd get a proper job. You said bartending is a proper job. Your mother said what kind of proper job finishes at three in the morning.
events.e_drunk: A table of drunk customers started a fight, a glass smashed on the bar and broken glass caught the back of your hand. You called the police, and at four in the morning you were still giving a statement at the station.
events.e_complaint: Someone from the neighborhood office came to say there had been twenty-odd noise complaints: no more music after midnight. After that the bar got a lot quieter, and so did business.
events.e_blackout: The whole street lost power and the bar was down to phone flashlights. You lit candles, kept the freezer going on the backup supply, and finished the three drinks already ordered. The customers said it was the best night they'd ever had there.
events.e_contest: You entered the Chengdu round of a national cocktail competition with a drink made from Sichuan peppercorn and jasmine tea, and came second. A judge said your drink tasted of Chengdu, and as soon as you got back you put it on the menu.
events.e_ambassador: A spirits brand's ambassador did a guest shift at the bar and brought a case of bottles you'd only read about. Before he left he pressed his card on you and said look him up in Shanghai some time.
events.e_rent: The landlord wanted thirty percent more rent. The owner haggled for a month and signed in the end. He said there'd be no raises for you this year. You nodded and went back to cutting ice.
events.e_stomach: Tasting every day and living upside down, your stomach went first. The endoscopy report said chronic gastritis. The doctor told you to drink less and eat on time. You smiled and said nothing.
events.e_insomnia: After years of nights for days, you started lying awake all night and feeling foggy in the day. The doctor called it a circadian rhythm disorder. You said my day is the night.
events.e_tourism: Chengdu got popular with tourists, the little bar became a check-in spot for visitors, and in a night you'd hear five or six accents. You learned a few lines of English to introduce the peppercorn drink.
events.e_wedding: You married at a farmhouse restaurant outside Chengdu and mixed every drink of the day yourself. Half the guests ended up under the table.
events.e_ai_menu: You started using AI to cost new drinks and work out margins, and it can predict from sales how many lemons to prep tomorrow. But the “guaranteed hit” it recommended, you made, tasted once, and poured away.
events.e_apprentice: Your apprentice worked the bar alone for the first time, hands shaking so much he could barely pick up the ice. You stood beside him and said nothing, until he pushed out the first drink and the customer said it was good.
events.e_renewal: The old street is being “renewed.” Slogans went up on the walls and two places next door have already closed. The owner said the street might become an influencer street, or it might become some other street.
events.e_rtd: The supermarkets started selling canned cocktails, a dozen yuan a can, and they keep getting better. A customer walked in and asked: what makes yours different from the convenience-store kind?
events.e_ai_order: The bar went over to ordering by QR code, and a screen now lines up the drinks for you. You get fewer chances to talk to customers, so you step out from behind the bar a little more.
events.e_regular_gone: That regular who came three times a week is moving away. On his last night he stayed till closing and ordered the same Old Fashioned, and as he left he said: wherever I drink from now on, I'll think of this one.
events.e_knees: Ten hours on your feet at a stretch, and your knees and back have begun to ache, with calluses on your soles. You bought proper non-slip shoes and soak your feet in hot water after work.

c_wset.title: Pay for the WSET Level 2 in spirits
c_wset.situation: A customer who knew his stuff told you your technique was good but your grasp of regions was shaky. The Level 2 spirits certificate costs over ¥4,000, plus weekend classes: just over a month's pay.

options.label: Sign up
options.result: You finished the course and blind-tasted your way through twenty-odd sample bottles in your rented room. The day you passed you sent your mother a photo of the certificate, and she asked what it was for.

options.label: No, learn behind the bar
options.result: You kept the money and learned bit by bit from the bottles regulars brought and from books. Once you got a spirit's region wrong, and that customer corrected you with a smile.

c_head.title: Become Head Bartender and take over the menu
c_head.situation: The owner wants you as Head Bartender: menu development, quality control and the apprentices, ¥1,000 more a month. The other bartender wants the job too, and he was here first.

options.label: Take it
options.result: You started writing the seasonal menu, testing each new drink dozens of times. The older bartender left two months later, and before he went he told you: your drinks are good, but you're too blunt.

options.label: Let the senior man have it
options.result: You stepped aside. He became head bartender, and you stayed at the other end of the bar making the drinks you wanted to make, sketching new menus in your notebook at weekends.

c_hotel.title: Move to a five-star hotel lounge
c_hotel.situation: The lounge of an international five-star hotel is hiring bartenders: social insurance, staff meals, no three a.m. finishes. But the menu is set by head office, and you'd wear a uniform, speak English and make every drink by the SOP.

options.label: Go to the hotel
options.result: You put on a waistcoat and bow tie and made the same martinis every night for business travelers. For the first time your social-insurance card had a record, and sometimes you missed the motley crowd on the old street.

options.label: Stay on the old street
options.result: You said you'd rather write your own menu. The lounge manager kept your number and said to call when you'd thought it over.

c_shanghai.title: Go to one of Shanghai's top cocktail bars
c_shanghai.situation: The brand ambassador recommends you to a Shanghai cocktail bar that's on the ranked lists, starting as a regular bartender: forty percent more pay, three times the rent. Two years there would change your résumé.

options.label: Go to Shanghai
options.result: In Shanghai you learned the centrifuge, the rotary evaporator and milk-washing, and how to make three hundred drinks in a night. You got thinner, and faster.

options.label: Stay in Chengdu
options.result: You didn't go. Chengdu nights are slow, the regulars are still here, and you tried every technique you'd seen online, one by one, at your own bar.

c_ai.title: Learn to build menus with AI, or not
c_ai.situation: A friend in the drinks business uses AI for flavor pairing and costing: ten new drink ideas in minutes, plus analysis of the reviews of every bar nearby. He tells you to learn it too; bartenders who can't will be left behind. You think flavor is something you have to taste yourself.

options.label: Learn it, let it draft
options.result: You let the AI draft ideas and made and tasted each one yourself; one in ten survived. Its margins were more accurate than yours, and for the first time you knew which drinks were losing money.

options.label: No, trust your tongue
options.result: You still write recipes by hand in your notebook and test each drink dozens of times. You don't create many, but every one is remembered.

c_own.title: Open a bar of your own
c_own.situation: A tiny noodle shop on the old street is up for transfer: twelve square meters, ¥300,000 for the lease and the fit-out. Your savings are less than half of that, and some regulars will lend you part. Open it and it's your own bar, and your own debt.

options.label: Open it, borrow if you must
options.result: You opened a bar with just six seats, and painted the sign yourself. In the first month you slept four hours a night, and the books were still in the red.

options.label: Wait a while
options.result: You didn't. The shop became a bubble-tea place, and you glance at it every time you pass.

c_ambassador.title: Become a spirits brand ambassador
c_ambassador.situation: A multinational spirits group is hiring a brand ambassador for the southwest: guest shifts at bars, classes for bartenders, pushing the company's bottles. Double the pay, no more nights behind one bar, but every drink you make has to use their spirits.

options.label: Become the ambassador
options.result: You picked up a case of bottles and started crisscrossing the southwest.
options.end: You do guest shifts at bar after bar in Kunming, Guiyang and Chongqing, standing behind someone else's counter, mixing a drink with a hint of Sichuan peppercorn and telling stories of three a.m. on an old Chengdu street.

options.label: Stay behind the bar
options.result: You said you still wanted to make the drinks you wanted to make. The job went to someone else, who later did a guest shift at your bar.

c_tea.title: Join a tea-drinks chain in product development
c_tea.situation: A national tea-drinks chain wants you as a beverage development consultant, bringing the layered flavors of the bar into milk tea: nine to six, with social insurance. Your recipes would be in thousands of shops, and nobody would know who made them.

options.label: Go into development
options.result: You moved into a lab full of measuring cylinders and digital scales.
options.end: Every day you mix dozens of samples in the lab. Now and then, out on the street, you see a young person holding the tea you designed. They take a sip, frown slightly, then take another.

options.label: Don't go
options.result: You said you still wanted to watch people drink. That night, behind the bar, you made one more drink, for yourself.

c_brand.title: A regular wants to invest and turn it into a brand
c_brand.situation: A regular in the restaurant business wants to put money in, turn your bar into a small brand and open three, with you as Beverage Development Director, in charge of menus and supply, no longer behind the bar every night. You know that once there are more bars, each drink is no longer one you made yourself.

options.label: Build the brand
options.result: You opened a second, then a third, and started writing SOPs, negotiating purchasing and sitting in meetings. One night on an inspection visit to the third bar, you sat on a customer's stool and drank a cocktail you hadn't made.

options.label: Keep just the one bar
options.result: You said one is enough. You're still behind the bar every night, and the regulars have gone from young people to middle-aged couples bringing their kids for alcohol-free drinks.

endings.retire: On the last night you make the last drinks for the last table of regulars, then wipe the bar spoon, the jigger and that ice pick clean and set each back in its place. Before turning off the lights you pour yourself a small one and drink it on a customer's stool. At three in the morning you lock the door, and the street is as quiet as on your very first night.
endings.burnout: That night after closing you were crouched behind the bar washing glasses, and when you stood up everything went black; you had to grab the freezer to stay on your feet. The doctor said your stomach and your sleep couldn't take this anymore. You handed the bar to your apprentice and started working days and sleeping nights, and when you pass the old street you still look in through that lit doorway.

past: You were at middle school in a small county town in Sichuan, with middling grades. What you liked best was helping out in the summer at your uncle's hotpot restaurant, watching grown-ups drink and talk, each table louder than the last.

You missed the cutoff for academic high school and went to a vocational school in the city to study hotel service. In the first mixology class the teacher tossed a cocktail shaker in the air and caught it, and the whole class cheered.

After vocational school you went to work as a waiter in a Chengdu hotpot restaurant: carrying pots, topping up broth, taking orders, twenty thousand steps a night. After work you often sat for a while in the little bar nearby, watching the people behind the counter.

That bar was hiring a barback. You applied, and when the owner asked what you could do, you said carry things and remember what customers like. You started out cutting ice, washing glasses and making syrup, for less than the hotpot place paid.

In the time after work you memorized fifty classic recipes, and in your rented room you practiced free-pouring with bottled water, fifteen, thirty, forty-five milliliters, until you could do it blind without missing.
The bartender left, and the owner had you cover for one night. You made ninety drinks without a single mistake, and the next day he said: this is your spot now.

late.pension_note: Estimate: bartenders mostly pay into social insurance themselves as flexible workers, on a low contribution base with gaps in the years, so the pension comes to a little over thirty percent of your final monthly pay.
scenes: For the first month of retirement you still didn't feel sleepy until three, and slept till noon. Slowly you learned to go to bed early, and for the first time saw the seven o'clock sun on the old estate.
Your apprentice opened a bar of his own and asked you to work the opening night. You made just one Old Fashioned, stirred until the glass fogged, and slid it to the first customer.
You set up a little bar on your balcony and at weekends make alcohol-free drinks for the old neighbors. They call you “boss,” and you don't correct them.
The old street's renewal is finished, and it's become a street you hardly recognize. You found where the bar used to be. It's a bookshop now, and the huangjue tree is still outside the door.
You found a day job at a café making pour-overs and cold brew. For the first few months you'd still come awake at ten at night and lie staring at the ceiling.
Your stomach slowly mended and you could taste a little alcohol again. Whenever your apprentice's bar has a new menu, he brings you a glass first, and you say only: too sweet, or: fine.

When the time came you retired, on a small pension. You taught a course at the community senior college, showing old people how to mix drinks from tea and fruit, and the waiting list ran to two terms.
In the first year away from the bar you'd wake in the small hours, your hands making the motion of a shake without you.
You found your feet in the new place. When you go back to Chengdu, hardly anyone on the old street knows you, except the owner of a maocai stall who still remembers you like extra peppercorns.

An apprentice you trained won a prize at a competition, and in his speech said his first teacher was on an old street in Chengdu. You watched the video on your phone. You didn't like it. You watched it twice.

Later, ordering, queueing and margins all went to machines, and even new drink ideas came at the press of a button. But the person at the bar who has just been left still needs someone to hand them a napkin.
There's a faint scar in the web of your right hand from chipping ice when you were young. A child asked what it was, and you said it was an ice ball that didn't come out quite round.

closing.retire: Many years later, on a summer night, you sit in a riverside teahouse and order jasmine tea. When it comes you breathe it in and remember the drink you once made with it. You don't order a drink. You just hold the tea and watch the lights on the river come on, one by one.
closing.burnout: Many years later you simmer a small pot of syrup in your kitchen with a few Sichuan peppercorns, and the whole flat fills with that smell. You pour it into an old bottle, label it, write the date, and put it in the fridge.
closing.end: Many years later, at the bottom of a trunk, you find your handwritten recipe book, its pages blotched with spilled drinks, and on the last page the name of the bar you never quite opened. You look at it for a while, then close the book.

stages: You work the bar alone now. Every night you make drinks to the house menu, Boston shaker, jigger and bar spoon never out of your hands, stirring an Old Fashioned until the glass fogs. When a regular sits down you hand them water first and ask whether they want something sharper or stronger, no jargon. Prep, drinks and clearing are all yours, and when something goes wrong, nobody covers for you.

You own the drinks at the main bar. Every day before opening you taste the syrups and juices and remake whatever is off; when the seasonal menu changes, you test recipes again and again with a digital scale and a probe thermometer, have the apprentice make them, and taste each one. Customers ask for you by name, and the owner starts asking you what to order next month.

You've stepped out from behind the bar. Every week you take stock against the till system and the inventory sheet, working out the wastage and margin on every bottle; you draw up rotas, train new staff, haggle with distributors, and deal with the neighborhood office and the landlord. You still work the bar, but more often you watch others work it, and you can spot a wrong drink at a glance.

Your job is the menus for several bars. Your days are full of meetings: with supply on custom syrups and ice, with brands on collaborations, with bar managers over the reports to see which drinks are losing money. Now and then you try something new in the lab with a rotary evaporator and a centrifuge, and when it's right you don't serve it yourself; you write it up as a standard recipe and send it to every bar.
work: A visitor in a suit ordered a Negroni in English. With the jigger you measured thirty milliliters each of gin, Campari and sweet vermouth. He took a sip and gave you a thumbs up.
The owner handed you a Japanese ice pick and a two-kilo block of ice and told you to carve twenty ice balls. The seventh was the first round one, and you'd worn a blister into your palm.
The designer regular from next door brought a whisky he'd carried back from Japan and asked for a highball with it. You adjusted the soda three times before he said: that's it.
The new apprentice never shook long enough. You put the probe thermometer into his drink: minus three. You said shake five more seconds, and strain at minus six.

For the new menu you weighed out twenty portions of peppercorn syrup on the digital scale, each two grams apart, lined them up for the owner and two regulars to taste blind, and chose number fourteen.
A distributor's rep brought a case of newly arrived mezcals. You poured each into a nosing glass, smelled them one by one, and ticked just one on his order form.

At the month-end stocktake, comparing the till report with the empties behind the bar, you found gin wastage ten percent higher than last month. The next day you replaced every jigger with graduated ones.
Someone from the neighborhood office came to check fire safety. You showed him the extinguishers and the exits, signed the inspection form, and poured him an alcohol-free lemon soda.

A new bartender worked his first Saturday night. You didn't go behind the bar; you stood in the corner and watched for two hours, and at the end of the night told him just one thing: one step less on every move.

In the lab you clarified a pot of tomato water in the centrifuge, made it into a clear Bloody Mary, and wrote it up as a standard recipe. The managers of three bars spent an afternoon learning it from the video.

A chain brand's marketing manager came to talk about a collaboration. Leafing through their product handbook, you struck out a line in the recipe clause of the contract and said the syrup has to be one we make ourselves.
The supply-chain manager brought a quote and asked whether to switch lemon suppliers next year. You had him send two cases of samples first, cut one open, smelled it, and said: no change.
